newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KL overnight steady after fall in interbank rates.
newsitem.headline: KL overnight steady after fall in interbank rates.

text.p: The overnight interbank rate was steady at 8.8/9.0 percent due to improved liquidity and a fall in interbank rates in the morning session, dealers said.
The overnight indicated that interbank rates were returning to normalcy after two weeks of turbulence in the foreign exchange markets.
The fall in rates started on Monday after heavy lending by big local banks in the one-month segment, said to be on behalf of the central bank.
No confirmation was available from Bank Negara Malaysia as it does not comment on its market intervention operations.
The intervention helped bring down the overnight rate to around nine percent on Monday from 18/20 before the weekend.
This brought down other interbank rates on Tuesday morning.
The dealers said movement of swaps to the left and continued lending by big banks aided in the easing of interbank rates.
One-week money was at 8.0/9.0 percent against 10/11 percent previously and two-week was at 8.0/9.0 percent against 9.0/11.0 percent.
One-month was at 7.5/8.0 percent against 8.5/9.0, while three-month and six-month were steady at 7.5/8.0 percent.
The overnight rate on Monday fell to 8.0/8.5 percent from 18/20 percent on Friday.
"It helped that swaps have also been moving left (or easing) in the last few days," said a dealer with another Malaysian bank.

One-month swaps were quoting at 35/40 points on Tuesday, which translated into an implied yield of 7.3/4 percent, dealers said. A few days ago one-month had touched a high of 500, which implied a yield of 20 percent.
"The swaps are back to normal and so are the interbank rates," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore.

He said the markets had calmed down after the interest rate rises caused by an aggressive central bank intervention to prevent the ringgit's fall two weeks ago. The central bank was said to have sold around $1 billion.
The intervention drained liquidity from the system, causing the market to be short, and interbank rates to rise to unusually high levels, dealers said.
Interest rate futures on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange were mixed as the selling triggered by interest rate falls were countered by covering of positions, futures dealers said.
At the close, the three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) contract for June 1997 was unchanged at 92.49, or an implied yield of 7.51 percent.
September 1997 contract was down one point at 92.60, or 7.40 percent and December was down two at 92.60, or 7.40 percent.
